However, the most commonly used topological filament finder, DisPerSE, faces a memory bottleneck: it requires a Delaunay tessellation of the full input point set, preventing application to large simulations. Naively splitting the volume fails, as different sub-volumes yield inconsistent tessellations and filament networks. We present a frozen-core method that overcomes this bottleneck while preserving the global topology. The volume is decomposed into overlapping blocks whose tessellations are filtered by a circumsphere criterion retaining only globally valid tetrahedra; a post-processing pipeline merges the tiled outputs through core filtering, deduplication, and boundary stitching. Validation against a monolithic reference on a $300\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ MDPL2 subvolume shows 99.6 per cent total length recovery, 100 per cent recovery of density maxima and minima, and 94.7 per cent individual filament matching (the ${\sim}$5 per cent of unmatched filaments are predominantly short, low-significance structures). We apply the method to the full $(1\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Gpc})^3$ MDPL2 box (92 million haloes), producing a gigaparsec-scale filament catalogue. As a first application, we measure the connectivity ($κ$) for 22,900 haloes spanning $M_{200\mathrm{c}} = 10^{12}$-$10^{15.5}\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$, finding a power-law mass-connectivity relation that extends from group to cluster scales, providing the first confirmation in an $N$-body halo catalogue that the theoretically predicted scaling holds across three decades in halo mass.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a frozen-core method to overcome the memory bottleneck of DisPerSE filament finding by decomposing volumes into overlapping blocks with circumsphere-filtered tessellations, achieving 99.6% length recovery. Applied to the full (1 Gpc)^3 MDPL2 simulation, it produces a gigaparsec-scale filament catalogue and confirms a power-law mass-connectivity relation across three decades in halo mass (10^12–10^15.5 h^−1 M⊙).
AI.motivation: DisPerSE, the most common topological filament finder, requires a Delaunay tessellation of the full input point set, creating a memory bottleneck that prevents its application to large simulations. Naive volume splitting fails because sub-volumes produce inconsistent tessellations and filament networks.
AI.method: A frozen-core method decomposes the volume into overlapping blocks; tessellations are filtered by a circumsphere criterion retaining only globally valid tetrahedra. A post-processing pipeline merges tiled outputs through core filtering, deduplication, and boundary stitching.
AI.result: Validation against a monolithic reference on a 300 h^−1 Mpc subvolume shows 99.6% total length recovery, 100% recovery of density maxima/minima, and 94.7% individual filament matching (unmatched filaments are short, low-significance). Applied to the full (1 h^−1 Gpc)^3 MDPL2 box (92 million haloes), producing a gigaparsec-scale filament catalogue.
AI.conclusion: Measurement of connectivity (κ) for 22,900 haloes (10^12–10^15.5 h^−1 M⊙) yields a power-law mass-connectivity relation extending from group to cluster scales, providing the first confirmation in an N-body halo catalogue that the theoretically predicted scaling holds across three decades in halo mass.

title: Spectral study of the outburst decay of the accreting millisecond X-ray pulsar SRGA J144459.2-604207
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures
summary: We study the spectra of the accreting X-ray millisecond pulsar SRGA J144459.2-604207 during the 2024 outburst using the Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer (NICER) and Swift observations. The spectra during the outburst decay, reflares, and quiescent state are explored using the absorbed Comptonized model. We find that the spectra during the quiescent state can also be explained using the absorbed power-law and absorbed blackbody model. The spectral evolution of the source is explored as the outburst decays into quiescence. We study the long-term quiescent X-ray activity of the source spanning roughly 45 years and find that the long-term quiescent luminosity may be explained using the deep crustal heating model. We also find that the coronal activity of the companion star alone cannot power the quiescent X-ray luminosity of the source. We place the source on the radio-X-ray luminosity plane and compare its position with other sources. We estimate the propeller luminosity of the source and find that it is smaller than the estimated luminosity during reflares and the quiescent state during the 2024 outburst. Several reflares are detected during the outburst decay, one of which is near-simultaneous with the detection of an ultrafast outflow and radio emission. We explore plausible mechanisms that may power outflow, radio emission and associated jet formation in this accreting binary.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes X-ray spectra of the accreting millisecond pulsar SRGA J144459.2-604207 during its 2024 outburst using NICER and Swift data, examining spectral evolution from outburst decay through quiescence, studying long-term quiescent activity over ~45 years, and investigating connections between outflows, radio emission, and jet formation.
AI.motivation: To understand the spectral evolution and physical mechanisms powering X-ray emission during outburst decay, reflares, and quiescence in the accreting millisecond pulsar SRGA J144459.2-604207, and to investigate long-term quiescent activity, propeller effects, and jet/outflow formation in this system.
AI.method: NICER and Swift observations; absorbed Comptonized model for spectra during outburst decay, reflares, and quiescence; absorbed power-law and blackbody models for quiescent spectra; long-term quiescent activity analysis over ~45 years; radio-X-ray luminosity plane comparison; propeller luminosity estimation.
AI.result: Quiescent spectra can be explained by absorbed power-law and blackbody models; long-term quiescent luminosity may be explained by deep crustal heating; companion star coronal activity alone cannot power quiescent X-ray luminosity; propeller luminosity is smaller than estimated luminosity during reflares and quiescence; several reflares detected, one near-simultaneous with ultrafast outflow and radio emission.
AI.conclusion: The source's long-term quiescent emission is likely powered by deep crustal heating; the propeller effect does not dominate during reflares and quiescence; the near-simultaneous detection of reflare, ultrafast outflow, and radio emission suggests a connection between accretion variability, outflows, and jet formation in this binary system.

title: Fuelling the central region of galaxies with misaligned gas accretion
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS. 15 pages, 13 figures
summary: Recent studies have shown that the accretion of kinematically misaligned gas fuels the central reservoir of galaxies, triggering nuclear activity and star formation. In this work, we show that this specific accretion channel can only sustain main-sequence levels of star formation in galaxies with $M_* \lesssim 10^{10} {\rm M_\odot}$. Using a sample of 201 kinematically misaligned galaxies, and a comparison sample of 3689 aligned galaxies, from the Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory survey, we investigate the impact of kinematically misaligned gas on star formation across stellar mass. We characterise the global specific star formation rate, central concentration and mass of ionized gas of our samples, and derive radial profiles of specific star formation rate and ionized gas mass surface density. We find that misaligned galaxies exhibit more centrally concentrated ionized gas than their aligned counterparts, with the strongest enhancement occurring at intermediate masses ($10^{10}$-$10^{10.6} {\rm M_\odot}$), where the central ionized gas density peaks. In galaxies less massive than $10^{10} {\rm M_\odot}$, misaligned gas fuels nuclear star formation at rates typical of star-forming systems. At higher masses, however, the impact of this newly accreted gas is diluted by the larger pre-existing stellar mass in the central regions, limiting its ability to rejuvenate the star formation activity in these galaxies. Our results also show that misaligned galaxies with or without nuclear activity exhibit similar central concentrations of ionized gas, suggesting that most have a reservoir capable of fuelling their supermassive black holes over timescales longer than typical nuclear activity episodes.

AI.tldr: Using 201 misaligned and 3689 aligned galaxies from MaNGA, this study finds that kinematically misaligned gas accretion sustains main-sequence star formation only in galaxies with M* ≲ 10¹⁰ M☉, with strongest effects at intermediate masses (10¹⁰–10¹⁰·⁶ M☉) where central ionized gas density peaks. At higher masses, dilution by pre-existing stars limits rejuvenation, while both active and inactive misaligned galaxies show similar gas concentrations capable of fueling SMBHs.
AI.motivation: To understand how kinematically misaligned gas accretion influences star formation and nuclear activity across different stellar mass regimes in galaxies.
AI.method: Comparative analysis of 201 kinematically misaligned galaxies versus 3689 aligned galaxies from the MaNGA survey, examining global sSFR, central concentration, radial profiles of sSFR, and ionized gas mass surface density across stellar mass.
AI.result: Misaligned galaxies have more centrally concentrated ionized gas; strongest enhancement at intermediate masses (10¹⁰–10¹⁰·⁶ M☉). Below 10¹⁰ M☉, misaligned gas sustains main-sequence star formation; above this threshold, dilution by pre-existing stellar mass limits star formation rejuvenation. Active and non-active misaligned galaxies show similar central gas concentrations.
AI.conclusion: Kinematically misaligned gas accretion is effective for sustaining star formation only in lower-mass galaxies (≲10¹⁰ M☉), while in more massive galaxies its impact is diluted. The similar gas concentrations suggest that misaligned galaxies generally have sufficient fuel for long-term SMBH feeding regardless of current activity.

title: When will T Coronae Borealis next erupt as a nova? Constraints from recurrence, orbital phase, and accretion-state evolution
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, Accepted for publication in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society Letter (MNRAS Letter)
summary: T Coronae Borealis (T CrB) is the nearest symbiotic recurrent nova and is now intensively monitored for its next eruption. We combine three constraints on the eruption time: historical recurrence, orbital phase, and recent accretion-state evolution. Conditioning on no eruption by 2026 July 11, the three effective historical intervals give illustrative survival-conditioned probabilities of 30.2\% for the rest of 2026 and 56.9\% within the following year; these are empirical indicators, not physical prediction probabilities. The four adopted historical eruption phases do not select a unique ignition phase, but form two loose pairs near $φ\simeq0.44$ and $φ\simeq0.62$, used here only as monitoring windows. The 1946 pre-eruption dip is difficult to explain by either a pure accretion-rate decline or standard dust extinction, and may have involved both accretion restructuring and source-dependent obscuration. If the renewed 2026 decline is the true pre-1946 analogue, an eruption around 2026 December remains plausible. Conversely, if post-2024 brightness remains below the 2014--2023 high state, an accretion-deficit estimate gives an earliest lower limit near 2029 May. The data therefore support conditional monitoring windows, not a unique date. These are conditional diagnostic scenarios rather than competing point predictions; the eventual eruption epoch will test their underlying assumptions.

AI.tldr: Three constraints (historical recurrence, orbital phase, accretion-state evolution) on T CrB's next eruption give a ~30% survival-conditioned probability for the rest of 2026 and ~57% within the following year, but these are empirical indicators, not point predictions. The 1946 pre-eruption dip may involve both accretion restructuring and source-dependent obscuration. If the 2026 decline mirrors 1946, an eruption around 2026 December is plausible; if post-2024 brightness stays low, the earliest limit is ~2029 May. The paper supports conditional monitoring windows, not a unique date.
AI.motivation: To constrain the timing of the next eruption of T Coronae Borealis (T CrB), the nearest symbiotic recurrent nova, which is being intensively monitored for its next outburst.
AI.method: Combining three constraints: historical recurrence intervals, orbital phase at eruption, and recent accretion-state evolution. Survival-conditioned probabilities are computed from empirical historical intervals, and two possible eruption-phase clusters (φ≈0.44 and φ≈0.62) are identified from four historical eruptions. The 1946 pre-eruption dip is analyzed to distinguish between accretion-rate decline and dust-extinction scenarios.
AI.result: Conditional on no eruption by 2026 July 11, survival-conditioned probabilities are ~30.2% for the rest of 2026 and ~56.9% within the following year. No unique ignition phase is selected; two loose pairs of eruption phases exist. The 1946 dip likely involves both accretion restructuring and source-dependent obscuration. If the 2026 decline mimics 1946, an eruption near 2026 December is plausible; if post-2024 brightness remains below the high state, an accretion-deficit lower limit gives ~2029 May.
AI.conclusion: The data support conditional monitoring windows and diagnostic scenarios rather than a unique prediction date. The eventual eruption epoch will test the underlying assumptions.

title: Discrepancies between Chandrasekhar's theory of relaxation and $N$-body simulations
comment: 13 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables, submitted to A&A
summary: Globular clusters are systems which are known to be particularly well described by two-body relaxation. In recent decades many studies have shown that Chandrasekhar's orbit-averaged theory is able to reproduce many features of numerical simulations. However, it has been claimed that differences between the theory and simulation remain, such as an amplitude mismatch of the rate of change of the distribution function. In this paper we compare the theoretical predictions of Chandrasekhar's theory for anisotropic clusters to precise $N$-body data. We show that more careful $N$-body measurements are able to reduce the claimed mismatch. Nevertheless, we observe a dependency of the remaining mismatch on both position and anisotropy. While the dependence on anisotropy may be understood qualitatively on theoretical grounds, the radial dependence implies that spatial inhomogeneities, and therefore collective effects, may become unavoidable to resolve the residual mismatch between theory and simulations.

AI.tldr: Chandrasekhar's orbit-averaged theory largely reproduces N-body simulations of globular clusters, but careful measurements reduce previously claimed mismatches; remaining position- and anisotropy-dependent discrepancies suggest collective effects may be needed for full resolution.
AI.motivation: To resolve the claimed mismatch between Chandrasekhar's orbit-averaged theory and N-body simulations for anisotropic globular clusters, and determine whether remaining discrepancies can be explained by measurement precision or require more fundamental theoretical extensions.
AI.method: Comparison of Chandrasekhar's orbit-averaged theory predictions with precise N-body simulation data for anisotropic globular clusters, with careful measurement techniques to minimize numerical artifacts.
AI.result: More careful N-body measurements reduce the previously claimed mismatch amplitude. However, a residual mismatch persists that depends on both radial position and anisotropy. The anisotropy dependence is qualitatively understandable theoretically, but the radial dependence suggests spatial inhomogeneities (collective effects) are needed.
AI.conclusion: Chandrasekhar's theory works better than previously thought when measurements are refined, but fully resolving the remaining theory-simulation discrepancy likely requires incorporating spatial inhomogeneities and collective effects beyond the orbit-averaged framework.

title: The COLIBRE-SKIRT pipeline: Calibration-free dust radiative transfer postprocessing for cosmological simulations
comment: Main text 23 pages and 8 figures. Submitted to A&A
summary: Context. Three-dimensional dust radiative transfer provides a powerful framework to connect cosmological galaxy simulations to multiwavelength observations. Until recently, in large-volume simulations, the formation of a cold ISM phase was prevented and dust was not evolved self-consistently. This required calibration of dust-to-metal ratios and extra subgrid dust attenuation in birth clouds, thereby reducing the predictive power. Aims. We present the COLIBRE-SKIRT pipeline, a calibration-free dust radiative transfer framework for the novel COLIBRE suite of large-volume cosmological simulations, which include a live dust model and directly simulate the multiphase ISM. Our primary aim is to establish a reference pipeline for generating multiwavelength mock observables from these simulations. As a first application, we produce far-ultraviolet (FUV) to far-infrared (FIR) spatially integrated spectra and assess them by comparison with the observed low-redshift cosmic spectral energy distribution (CSED). Methods. We apply the SKIRT dust radiative transfer code to the COLIBRE simulations. Dust masses and species fractions are taken directly from the simulation, and no birth cloud model is added in postprocessing. We introduce a "split & scale" approach that maps the simulated two-size, multi-species dust distribution onto continuous grain size distributions without introducing free parameters. Results. We find that, for the first time, a large-volume cosmological simulation directly reproduces the local Universe CSED without calibrating the postprocessing routine a priori. Residual tensions in the mid-infrared (~0.2 dex) point towards insufficient heating of the hottest dust components and uncertainties in the modelling of the PAH-emission carriers. This framework can be readily applied at low and high redshift to create synthetic spectra and images from the FUV to the FIR.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the COLIBRE-SKIRT pipeline, a calibration-free dust radiative transfer framework for cosmological simulations that directly reproduces the observed low-redshift cosmic spectral energy distribution from FUV to FIR without requiring a priori calibration of dust parameters or subgrid birth cloud models.
AI.motivation: Previous large-volume cosmological simulations required calibration of dust-to-metal ratios and extra subgrid dust attenuation in birth clouds because they lacked a cold ISM phase and self-consistently evolved dust, reducing predictive power. The authors aim to establish a calibration-free reference pipeline for generating multiwavelength mock observables.
AI.method: The SKIRT dust radiative transfer code is applied to COLIBRE simulations that include a live dust model and multiphase ISM. Dust masses and species fractions come directly from simulation without birth cloud postprocessing. A "split & scale" approach maps the simulated two-size, multi-species dust distribution onto continuous grain size distributions without introducing free parameters.
AI.result: For the first time, a large-volume cosmological simulation directly reproduces the local Universe CSED without calibrating the postprocessing routine a priori. Residual tensions (~0.2 dex) persist in the mid-infrared, indicating insufficient heating of the hottest dust components and uncertainties in PAH-emission carrier modelling.
AI.conclusion: The COLIBRE-SKIRT pipeline provides a calibration-free dust radiative transfer framework that can be readily applied at low and high redshift to create synthetic spectra and images from FUV to FIR, enabling direct comparison between cosmological simulations and multiwavelength observations.

title: The Goldilocks Molecule: H$_{2}$ Emission Lines Can Identify Elusive Dwarf AGN
comment: Accepted to RNAAS
summary: We propose using H$_{2}$ emission lines as a novel diagnostic to identify dwarf AGN by running photoionization models incorporating active intermediate-mass black holes and using an observed WISE dwarf AGN as a template. Though many dwarf AGN would be incorrectly classified as star-forming if the H$_{2}$~2.12~$μ$m/Br$γ$ ratio is used, ratios between H$_{2}$ emission lines can reveal active IMBHs in cases where log $n_{\text{H}} \gtrsim 4.0$. This includes the case where $M_{\text{BH}} = 10^3~M_{\odot}$, even though the optical strong lines and NIR coronal lines would likely go undetected. We conclude that H$_{2}$ emission lines show promise in detecting the most elusive IMBHs.

AI.tldr: H₂ emission lines are proposed as a novel diagnostic to identify dwarf AGN with intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs), particularly effective when hydrogen density log nₕ ≳ 4.0, even when optical and NIR coronal lines go undetected.
AI.motivation: Current diagnostics often misclassify dwarf AGN as star-forming, and detecting the most elusive intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) remains challenging with traditional optical and NIR coronal lines.
AI.method: Photoionization models incorporating active intermediate-mass black holes were run, using an observed WISE dwarf AGN as a template, to analyze H₂ emission line ratios as diagnostics.
AI.result: H₂ 2.12 μm/Brγ ratios often misclassify dwarf AGN as star-forming, but ratios between different H₂ emission lines can reveal active IMBHs when log nₕ ≳ 4.0, even for M_BH = 10³ M⊙ where optical strong lines and NIR coronal lines remain undetected.
AI.conclusion: H₂ emission lines are a promising diagnostic for detecting the most elusive IMBHs that are otherwise invisible to traditional line diagnostics.

title: Isomer-specific excitation of formic acid in collisions with helium atoms
summary: An accurate estimation of the molecular abundances of isomers in the interstellar medium (ISM) is necessary to unravel the underlying chemistry and physics. After the recent detections of both isomers of formic acid ($cis-$ and $trans-$HCOOH) in dense dark cold clouds, their accurate molecular line modeling became of interest. The conditions of these environments do not necessarily follow the local thermodynamic equilibrium, thus taking into account the competition between the radiative and collisional processes is required. This involves the knowledge of the rotational excitation data for collisions with the most abundant interstellar species \textemdash He and H$_2$. In this paper, the first potential energy surfaces (PES) for the interaction of the two rotamers of formic acid with He atoms are computed using the explicitly correlated coupled-cluster theory [CCSD(T)-F12]. The obtained PESs demonstrate qualitative similarities and high anisotropy. The global minima are found with $V=-53.0$ cm$^{-1}$ and $V=-46.0$ cm$^{-1}$ for $cis-$HCOOH and $trans-$HCOOH respectively. Collisional excitation cross sections calculated for total energies up to 100 cm$^{-1}$ demonstrate similar propensity rules for both isomers. Quantitative differences of the cross sections associated with the two rotamers are also discussed.

AI.tldr: First PES for cis- and trans-HCOOH with He using CCSD(T)-F12; collisional excitation cross sections computed up to 100 cm⁻¹ show similar propensity rules but quantitative differences between rotamers.
AI.motivation: Accurate estimation of molecular abundances of formic acid isomers in the ISM requires non-LTE modeling, which needs collisional excitation data with He/H₂.
AI.method: CCSD(T)-F12 theory used to compute first PESs for cis- and trans-HCOOH interacting with He; collisional excitation cross sections calculated up to 100 cm⁻¹.
AI.result: PESs show high anisotropy; global minima at V=-53.0 cm⁻¹ (cis) and V=-46.0 cm⁻¹ (trans). Cross sections show similar propensity rules but quantitative differences between the two rotamers.
AI.conclusion: The computed PES and cross sections enable accurate non-LTE modeling of formic acid isomers in cold dense clouds.

title: The World Cup in space: Finding ionised buckyballs in the ISM with CARMENES
comment: To appear in Highlights of Spanish Astrophysics XIII, Proceedings of the XVII Scientific Meeting of the Spanish Astronomical Society held on 13-17 July 2026, in Tarragona, Spain
summary: Over a century after the discovery of the first diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs) in absorption in stellar spectra (Heger et al 1922), their origin is still mostly unknown. The exception are four DIBs (out of 600+ known) in the 9300-9700 Angstrom region, for which a possible ascription to C_60^+ (ionised buckminsterfullerene, shaped liked a football, hence buckyballs) has been made. However, those DIBs are located in a spectral region heavily contaminated by telluric H_2O absorption, hampering their detection and study from the ground. I present the results of a study with the CARMENES spectrograph that uses a novel technique with multi-epoch spectroscopy at different times of the year to shift the relative position of the DIBs and the surrounding telluric lines, hence facilitating the analysis of the DIBs. The technique has been applied to 41 sightlines of diverse extinctions and environments, with positive detections in all of them. Our results are consistent with three of those DIBs having C_60^+ as the carrier.

AI.tldr: This study uses multi-epoch spectroscopy with the CARMENES spectrograph to analyze four diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs) in the 9300-9700 Å region potentially associated with C_60^+. By shifting relative positions of DIBs and telluric H₂O lines at different observation times, the technique enables detection across 41 sightlines, confirming three DIBs are consistent with C_60^+ as the carrier.
AI.motivation: Most of the 600+ known diffuse interstellar bands remain unidentified after a century, except for four DIBs potentially attributed to C_60^+. However, these DIBs are in a spectral region heavily contaminated by telluric H₂O absorption, making ground-based detection and study difficult.
AI.method: A novel multi-epoch spectroscopic technique using the CARMENES spectrograph was employed, taking observations at different times of the year to shift the relative positions of DIBs and telluric H₂O lines, thereby facilitating DIB analysis.
AI.result: The technique was applied to 41 sightlines with diverse extinctions and environments, yielding positive detections in all of them. Three of the four DIBs are consistent with C_60^+ as the carrier.
AI.conclusion: The multi-epoch technique successfully overcomes telluric contamination, enabling robust detection and analysis of C_60^+-associated DIBs across varied interstellar environments, supporting the identification of C_60^+ as the carrier for three of the four DIBs.

title: Berkeley 32: A Metal-poor and Dynamically Evolved Open Cluster with Evidence of Radial Migration
comment: 27 pages, including 15 figures and 4 tables, accepted for publication in the The Astronomical Journal (AJ)
summary: We present a comprehensive chemo-dynamical analysis of the old, metal-poor open cluster Berkeley 32 based on Gaia DR3 astrometry and Gaia-ESO Survey DR5.1 spectroscopy. Cluster membership is determined using a Gaussian Mixture Model applied to proper-motion components and trigonometric parallaxes. Isochrone fitting yields an age of 4.9 +/- 0.5 Gyr, a heliocentric distance of 3325 pc, and an extinction of A_V = 0.38 +/- 0.12 mag. Spectroscopic member stars exhibit a mean metallicity of [Fe/H] = -0.39 +/- 0.02 dex, near-solar alpha-element abundances, and a weighted mean radial velocity of V_rad = 106.26 +/- 0.03 km s^-1. The [Y/Mg] chemical clock yields an age of 4.73 +/- 2.39 Gyr, consistent with the isochrone estimate. Orbital integration indicates a moderately eccentric orbit (e = 0.268 +/- 0.004) with a guiding radius of R_g = 8.82 kpc. The inferred chemical birth radius, R_b = 9.82 kpc, together with DeltaR ~ -1 kpc, suggests moderate inward radial migration, while the offsets among R_b, R_g, and R_GC are consistent with both churning and blurring processes. A photometric analysis identifies a binary fraction of f_b = 0.449 +/- 0.017 for systems with mass ratios q >= 0.5, implying a substantial unresolved binary population. Radial cumulative distribution functions further reveal significant mass segregation, with evolved stars more centrally concentrated than main-sequence stars. These results indicate that Berkeley 32 is a dynamically evolved old-disk cluster whose present-day structure and orbit preserve signatures of both internal dynamical evolution and radial migration within the Galactic disk.

AI.tldr: Berkeley 32 is a dynamically evolved, metal-poor old open cluster (age ~4.9 Gyr, [Fe/H] = -0.39) showing moderate inward radial migration, mass segregation, and a high binary fraction (f_b = 0.449).
AI.motivation: To perform a comprehensive chemo-dynamical analysis of the old, metal-poor open cluster Berkeley 32 using Gaia DR3 astrometry and Gaia-ESO Survey DR5.1 spectroscopy, investigating its age, metallicity, kinematics, orbital history, and internal dynamical state.
AI.method: Gaussian Mixture Model for cluster membership (proper motions + parallaxes); isochrone fitting for age, distance, extinction; chemical clock ([Y/Mg]) for independent age estimate; orbital integration; photometric binary analysis; radial cumulative distribution functions for mass segregation.
AI.result: Age = 4.9 ± 0.5 Gyr; distance = 3325 pc; [Fe/H] = -0.39 ± 0.02 dex; near-solar [α/Fe]; V_rad = 106.26 ± 0.03 km/s; [Y/Mg] age = 4.73 ± 2.39 Gyr; e = 0.268 ± 0.004; R_g = 8.82 kpc; R_b = 9.82 kpc, ΔR ≈ -1 kpc (inward migration); binary fraction f_b = 0.449 ± 0.017 (q ≥ 0.5); mass segregation present.
AI.conclusion: Berkeley 32 is a dynamically evolved old-disk cluster whose present-day structure and orbit preserve signatures of both internal dynamical evolution (mass segregation, binary population) and radial migration (churning and blurring) within the Galactic disk.

title: Cluster characteristics of Galactic open clusters
comment: 11 pages, 17 figures, submitted to A&A
summary: Star clusters are perfectly suited for studying the formation, evolution, and dynamics of stars and their host galaxies. For this, we need to estimate total masses, radii and shapes of star clusters. These parameters strongly influence their fates in the host galaxies. However, there is no agreement about these characteristics in the literature. The published values widely disagree. We estimated total masses and cluster radii using a very conservative approach: calculating member masses and summing them. Furthermore, we investigated the three-dimensional characteristics of open clusters and their limitations. We used a commonly used grid of evolutionary tracks for different photometric sources, including 2MASS, Gaia, and Pan-STARRS. The interpolation method was tested using synthetic clusters built with ASteCA. To estimate three-dimensional shapes, we used the distribution of the well-known Galactic coordinates and inverse parallaxes. We estimated the total masses and radii of about 7000 open clusters and observed traces of tidal tails. Individual values can be used in future $Gaia$ data releases to obtain even more precise values. The current DR3 allows the study of only three-dimensional shapes up to 500 pc. Beyond this distance, we find a significant needle-like shape due to uncertainties in observed parallaxes.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes ~7000 open clusters using a conservative member-summing approach to estimate total masses, radii, and 3D shapes from 2MASS, Gaia, and Pan-STARRS data. Three-dimensional shape analysis is reliable only up to 500 pc due to parallax uncertainties causing needle-like artifacts beyond that distance. Traces of tidal tails are observed.
AI.motivation: Star cluster parameters (mass, radius, shape) strongly influence their evolution and fate in host galaxies, but published values in the literature widely disagree, necessitating a consistent and conservative estimation approach.
AI.method: Conservative member mass summation; interpolation method tested with synthetic clusters via ASteCA; 3D shapes estimated from Galactic coordinates and inverse parallaxes; grid of evolutionary tracks applied to 2MASS, Gaia, and Pan-STARRS photometry.
AI.result: Total masses and radii estimated for ~7000 open clusters; tidal tail traces observed; 3D shapes only reliable within 500 pc; beyond 500 pc, parallax uncertainties produce a needle-like shape artifact.
AI.conclusion: Current Gaia DR3 enables 3D shape studies up to 500 pc; future data releases may yield more precise values; the conservative mass summation approach provides consistent cluster parameters for future dynamical studies.
